drip.author: offsidewinger
drip.title: First beer league skate of the season. The lungs showed up. The hands did not get the memo.
drip.body:
Update for anyone who remembers me gasping through a summer drop-in: I did the dryland. Not perfectly. Realistically I got about nine good weeks of bike intervals and sled pushes, then a patchy August where the bike mostly held shirts.

First skate back was last night and I got through every shift without the second-shift gasp. Sat on the bench breathing like a normal person while a couple of the guys who skipped summer were folded over the boards. Didn't say anything. Didn't have to. Smugness is best served silently.

The hands, however, are exactly as bad as they were in the spring. Two passes off my skate and one into the bench door. Dryland fixes a lot of things. Not that.

comments.author: kettlebellkate
comments.body: Nine good weeks and a patchy August still adds up to the best-conditioned version of you that has ever started a season. Your legs don't keep track of which weeks were pretty. Proud of this one.

comments.author: penaltyboxphil
comments.body: Hands of stone is a lifetime condition. Lungs are fixable. You fixed the fixable one, and now you're out there long enough to make mistakes that nobody could see before.

replies.author: offsidewinger
replies.body: The bench said the same thing, with more swearing and less kindness.

comments.author: deadlift_diaries
comments.body: What I tell the hockey guys at my gym: keep one short strength day through the whole season instead of dropping it when games start. Two or three lifts, nothing heroic. The ones who stop in October are always asking where their legs went by February.

comments.author: half_marathon_harold
comments.body: The pass into the bench door is going to stay with me. Otherwise a genuinely great comeback arc. Enjoy having a whole season ahead of you. I'm a few weeks out from a race and every twinge in my body has become breaking news.

drip.author: half_marathon_harold
drip.title: Last long run before the taper: 18 km, 8 degrees, and the fall dividend finally paid out
drip.body:
Three weeks out from the October half. Went out at 7 this morning wearing gloves for the first time since spring and ran the same 18 km loop that had me crawling home through the soup all summer. Same effort. Almost four minutes faster overall. Heart rate stayed polite the entire way.

Somebody in here promised back in the heat that one cool morning I'd run like I'd been swapped for a better athlete. This was that morning. All those slow, sweaty, humbling summer runs were apparently deposits.

Now comes the taper, which is the part I'm worst at. Less running, more free time, and a brain that reads rest as falling behind. How do the rest of you survive the last couple of weeks before something you've trained for?

comments.author: protein_pancake
comments.body: That was me! The swapped-for-a-better-athlete morning! I'm unreasonably happy it showed up for you. Now go eat something large.

comments.author: kettlebellkate
comments.body: From the lifting side: treat the taper like a deload with a finish line. You're not losing anything in two weeks. You're letting everything you built settle in so it's all there on race day.

replies.author: half_marathon_harold
replies.body: A deload with a finish line. Writing that on the fridge so taper brain has something to read at 6 a.m.

comments.author: deadlift_diaries
comments.body: Meet prep has the exact same madness. What worked for me was giving the restless energy a job that isn't training. Clean the garage. Plan race morning down to the socks. Just don't touch the training plan.

comments.author: offsidewinger
comments.body: 18 km before most people have had a coffee. I'd need a Zamboni ride for the last ten. Good luck in October, the dressing room is rooting for you.

drip.author: kettlebellkate
drip.title: The light's going. Make your winter training plan now, while it's still bright out at supper.
drip.body:
Every year it goes the same way. September feels great, October gets dark, and by November half the people who were crushing it all summer have quietly stopped. It isn't laziness. The plan was built for long evenings and nobody updated it.

So I write the winter version now, while I'm still motivated enough to be honest. Three questions. Where does each session happen when it's dark and cold? For me the spare kettlebell moves out of the closet and onto the living room floor where I can see it. What's the minimum session for a bad week? Mine is ten minutes, and ten minutes counts as a full day on the calendar. What do I need before I need it? Headlamp, gloves, the boring stuff.

September me has sunlight and optimism, so September me makes the decisions. November me just follows the notes. What's in your winter plan?

comments.author: protein_pancake
comments.body: My winter plan is identical to my summer plan, which is the whole point of having one boring plan. The only change is a headlamp for the walk to the gym, because 5:45 is about to get very dark.

comments.author: goalie_mom_deb
comments.body: Hockey mom winter plan: the rink parking lot squats from the summer are moving inside to the lobby stairs. 5 a.m. practice, forty minutes of waiting, one staircase. My daughter has already asked me to please use a different entrance.

replies.author: kettlebellkate
replies.body: Rink stairs at 5 a.m. are elite programming. Nobody at a rink that early is judging anyone. They're all just trying to find the coffee.

comments.author: half_marathon_harold
comments.body: Reflective vest and a running club. Dark mornings are a lot easier when there are six people standing in a parking lot waiting for you and they know your name.

comments.author: deadlift_diaries
comments.body: The ten-minute floor is the whole plan. On the bad days I do the warm-up and one working set and write 'showed up' in the notebook. The ten minutes were never the point. The streak not breaking is the point.

drip.author: deadlift_diaries
drip.title: Read back through five years of one-line training notes. Every September says the same thing.
drip.body:
I've written one line after every session for about five years. This week I went back and read only the Septembers.

Every single year: 'Felt amazing.' 'Added weight.' 'Could have done more.' And every single November: 'Tired.' 'Elbows cranky.' 'Skipped, no energy.' Five years running I came back from summer feeling great, piled on too much too fast because it felt easy, and paid for it before the snow.

So this year September me gets a speed limit. Small jumps only, even when the bar feels light. Especially when the bar feels light. I don't trust a great month anymore. I trust a boring one.

If you don't keep notes, start. Your past self is the only coach who's watched every session.

comments.author: kettlebellkate
comments.body: The September overreach is back-to-school energy for adults. New notebook, new pencils, add twenty kilos. The speed limit is the right call.

comments.author: offsidewinger
comments.body: Beer league version: the first three games at full speed like I'm twenty-two, and by game four my groin is filing paperwork. Might need to start writing things down so I can read the evidence against myself.

replies.author: deadlift_diaries
replies.body: Write it down. Future you will read it and recognize the pattern, and recognizing it is most of the fix.

comments.author: protein_pancake
comments.body: I don't keep a notebook, but I've eaten pancakes at 7 after every session for three years, so technically my grocery receipts are a training log. Septembers show a lot of maple syrup.

drip.author: protein_pancake
drip.title: Added one Sunday walk to my routine and it's somehow become the best session of the week
drip.body:
For three years my routine has been the same lifts, same days, same 6am, and I defend it loudly. But at the end of the summer I added one thing: a long walk on Sunday mornings. No step goal, no pace, no planned route. Just an hour outside.

Turns out I needed one session with no numbers in it. The leaves are turning, it's cold enough for a hoodie, and I get home with a quieter head than any other day of the week. Didn't change anything in the gym and I'm sleeping better. Might be the walk, might be coincidence, I'm not running a study.

Anyone else have a session that exists purely because it feels good?

comments.author: kettlebellkate
comments.body: Every good routine needs one session that's for you and not for the spreadsheet. The most routine person I know finding room for a walk with no numbers in it makes me very happy.

comments.author: half_marathon_harold
comments.body: Easy runs are supposed to be exactly this and most runners ruin them by staring at their pace. My Sunday recovery run is watch-free now too. The goose is still out there though, so the shoes stay double-knotted.

replies.author: protein_pancake
replies.body: Watch-free recovery run with optional goose-based intervals. Very balanced program.

comments.author: offsidewinger
comments.body: Mine is Sunday shinny once the outdoor rinks open. Nobody keeps score, nobody's watching the clock, and I come home happier than after any league game. Until then I suppose I'll try walking like a civilian.

late_comments.author: offsidewinger
late_comments.body: Found this again while figuring out what to keep now that the season's started. Cut the dryland down to one short strength day a week and I'm going to run it, boring, until the playoffs. November me might actually be upright for once.

late_comments.author: kettlebellkate
late_comments.body: Came back to this after my first properly cold morning session. Same weights, same warm-up, and everything moved noticeably faster than it did all summer. The heat tax got refunded. Anyone stuck in a hot-weather slump earlier this year: this thread was right.
